weeks.weekName: The Progressive Era and American empire

pieces.text: In the mid-1800s,

—the belief that the U.S. was culturally superior and destined to expand its land and influence—led the country to expand its borders to the west. By 1890, Americans had settled enough western lands for the U.S. Census Bureau to declare that there was no longer a western frontier. In 1893, historian Frederick Jackson Turner expressed concern about the end of the frontier. Read an excerpt from Turner's essay. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: This perennial rebirth…this expansion westward with its new opportunities…[defines] American character…. So long as free land exists, the opportunity for a competency exists, and economic power secures political power….

Since the days when the fleet of Columbus sailed into the waters of the New World, America has been another name for opportunity…. the American energy will continually demand a wider field for its exercise. But never again will such gifts of free land offer themselves….

And now, four centuries from the discovery of America, at the end of a hundred years of life under the Constitution, the frontier has gone, and with its going has closed the first period of American history.

contents.text: Based on the excerpt, why would Turner be concerned that there was no longer a western frontier for the U.S. to explore?

choices.text: The loss of the frontier would prevent the U.S. from achieving greater equality during the next period of its history.
The loss of the frontier would lead to a Constitutional crisis during the next period of American history.
Expansion had helped Americans avoid confrontations, so without it, the likelihood of wars would increase.
Without the western frontier, the U.S. could lose its sense of purpose and opportunity for political and economic growth.

He also says that, "So long as free land exists," the opportunity exists to develop greater economic and political power. So, Turner believes that

content.text: without the western frontier, the U.S. could lose its sense of purpose and opportunity for political and economic growth

pieces.text: . Turner seems to mourn the closure of the frontier, suggesting that the nation must now grapple with finding new sources of energy, purpose, and growth.

subheader.text: Was the frontier really the defining feature of the country's identity?

subpoints.text: It depends who you ask. Turner believed frontier life forced settlers to be self-reliant and resourceful, fostering an American culture of individualism and democratic ideals. But Turner's thesis has been widely debated. Critics argue it oversimplifies the American experience and ignores the devastating impact on Native American communities. Native people experienced forced relocation, a loss of ancestral lands and sacred buffalo herds, and a profound disruption to indigenous ways of life.

, the practice of extending political, military, economic, and cultural control over other nations or territories, gained widespread support.

contents.text: Look back to the excerpts. These choices are correct:

content.text: They claimed it was God's will for them to spread their religion and civilization across the globe.

explanationText.text: Josiah Strong argued that "God, with infinite wisdom and skill, is training the Anglo-Saxon race for an hour sure to come in the world's future." He thought it was God's will that the people in the U.S. should spread their institutions, meaning their religion and way of life, around the world.

content.text: They argued that the English language, religion, and government were morally superior to other societies.

explanationText.text: John Fiske thought the "English race" was so superior that the rest of the world was destined to "become English in its language, in its religion, in political habits and traditions." Once the U.S. had political control over a new territory, imperialists expected the people to adopt their way of life.

contents.text: These choices are not correct:

content.text: They argued that imperialism was a cultural exchange that provided mutual opportunities for sharing ideas.

explanationText.text: Both Strong and Fiske considered other cultures to be less advanced. So, their views contradict the idea that imperialism was a cultural exchange to share ideas.

content.text: They claimed imperialism would preserve the local traditions and religious beliefs of the people who were colonized.

explanationText.text: Once the U.S. had political control over a new territory, imperialists expected the people to also adopt U.S. culture. So, this was not a way people tried to justify imperialism.

content.text: The U.S. needs to be able to sell its excess food supply and goods overseas.

explanationText.text: Beveridge states that the U.S. is growing more crops and making more goods than it can use. Beveridge also says "we must find new markets for our produce," which means finding new places to sell things that the U.S. produces.

contents.text: Beveridge says the U.S. is already "raising more [crops] than we can consume," which means producing more food than it needs. So, these choices are not correct:

content.text: The U.S. needs new territories to provide raw materials in order to increase its food supply.
The U.S. needs food from other countries because the U.S. does not raise enough crops.

pieces.text: In the late 19th century, military and political leaders increasingly pushed the U.S. toward imperialism. Some of these leaders drew on the ideas of
, a widely respected naval officer and military historian. Read the passage describing some of Mahan's ideas. Then answer the question below.
Captain Alfred Mahan urged the U.S. to build a more powerful navy. His 1890 book,

content.text: The Influence of Sea Power upon History

pieces.text: , argued that a nation's economic prosperity, political influence, and military power depended on control of the world's seaways. He believed that control of the seas would increase U.S. influence globally and help the U.S. expand into new markets. To become a major naval power, Mahan argued the U.S. needed to replace its wooden ships with modern steel vessels fueled by coal and oil, and then build naval bases in ports across the globe for refueling both merchant and naval ships.

contents.text: How could Mahan's plans to strengthen the navy contribute to the U.S. becoming an imperial power?

Additional funding would allow the navy to build new wooden ships for U.S. merchants to transport their goods overseas.

Building more naval bases in the U.S. could help stop the flow of imported goods from foreign countries.

contents.text: This choice is correct:

content.text: With a stronger military, the U.S. could intervene in overseas conflicts to protect and promote its interests.

explanationText.text: The passage says that Mahan "believed that control of the seas would increase U.S. influence globally and help the U.S. expand into new markets." His vision of a strong navy laid the foundation for the U.S. to become a dominant imperial power.

contents.text: The other choices are not correct:

content.text: Modern naval ships could be used instead of merchant ships to transport goods to both domestic and foreign markets.

explanationText.text: The passage does not say that the navy ships would be used instead of merchant ships for trade. Mahan believed the U.S. needed a strong navy to control the seas and protect U.S. merchant ships transporting goods on international trade routes.

content.text: Additional funding would allow the navy to build new wooden ships for U.S. merchants to transport their goods overseas.

pieces.text: Mahan wanted the navy to build new
ships to replace the wooden ships in its fleet. The passage does not say anything about the navy making new ships for U.S. merchants.

content.text: Building more naval bases in the U.S. could help stop the flow of imported goods from foreign countries.

explanationText.text: Mahan wanted the navy to build international naval bases "in ports across the globe" that merchant ships could use for refueling. The passage does not mention using the U.S. Navy to stop foreign trade.

In the mid-1800s,

—the belief that the U.S. was culturally superior and destined to expand its land and influence—led the country to expand its borders to the west. By 1890, Americans had settled enough western lands for the U.S. Census Bureau to declare that there was no longer a western frontier. In 1893, historian Frederick Jackson Turner expressed concern about the end of the frontier. Read an excerpt from Turner's essay. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: This perennial rebirth…this expansion westward with its new opportunities…[defines] American character…. So long as free land exists, the opportunity for a competency exists, and economic power secures political power….

Since the days when the fleet of Columbus sailed into the waters of the New World, America has been another name for opportunity…. the American energy will continually demand a wider field for its exercise. But never again will such gifts of free land offer themselves….

And now, four centuries from the discovery of America, at the end of a hundred years of life under the Constitution, the frontier has gone, and with its going has closed the first period of American history.

pieces.text: . Turner seems to mourn the closure of the frontier, suggesting that the nation must now grapple with finding new sources of energy, purpose, and growth.

subheader.text: Was the frontier really the defining feature of the country's identity?

subpoints.text: It depends who you ask. Turner believed frontier life forced settlers to be self-reliant and resourceful, fostering an American culture of individualism and democratic ideals. But Turner's thesis has been widely debated. Critics argue it oversimplifies the American experience and ignores the devastating impact on Native American communities. Native people experienced forced relocation, a loss of ancestral lands and sacred buffalo herds, and a profound disruption to indigenous ways of life.

In his essay, Turner says that "expansion westward with its new opportunities" has defined the American character, but the western frontier is now gone. He also says that, "So long as free land exists," the opportunity exists to develop greater economic and political power. So, Turner believes that without the western frontier, the U.S. could lose its

content.text: sense of purpose and opportunity for political and economic growth

pieces.text: . Turner seems to mourn the closure of the frontier, suggesting that the nation must now grapple with finding new sources of energy, purpose, and growth.

subheader.text: Was the frontier really the defining feature of the country's identity?

subpoints.text: It depends who you ask. Turner believed frontier life forced settlers to be self-reliant and resourceful, fostering an American culture of individualism and democratic ideals. But Turner's thesis has been widely debated. Critics argue it oversimplifies the American experience and ignores the devastating impact on Native American communities. Native people experienced forced relocation, a loss of ancestral lands and sacred buffalo herds, and a profound disruption to indigenous ways of life.

In 1893, historian Frederick Jackson Turner expressed concern about the end of the frontier. Read an excerpt from Turner's essay. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: This perennial rebirth…this expansion westward with its new opportunities…[defines] American character…. So long as free land exists, the opportunity for a competency exists, and economic power secures political power….

Since the days when the fleet of Columbus sailed into the waters of the New World, America has been another name for opportunity…. the American energy will continually demand a wider field for its exercise. But never again will such gifts of free land offer themselves….

And now, four centuries from the discovery of America, at the end of a hundred years of life under the Constitution, the frontier has gone, and with its going has closed the first period of American history.

contents.text: Based on the excerpt, why would Turner be concerned that there was no longer a western frontier for the U.S. to explore?

choices.text: The loss of the frontier would prevent the U.S. from achieving greater equality during the next period of its history.
Expansion had helped Americans avoid confrontations, so without it, the likelihood of wars would increase.
Without the western frontier, the U.S. could lose its sense of purpose and opportunity for political and economic growth.
The loss of the frontier would lead to a Constitutional crisis during the next period of American history.

pieces.text: In his essay, Turner says that "expansion westward with its new opportunities" has defined the American character, but the western frontier is now gone. He also says that, "So long as free land exists," the opportunity exists to develop greater economic and political power. So, Turner believes that

content.text: without the western frontier, the U.S. could lose its sense of purpose and opportunity for political and economic growth

pieces.text: . Turner seems to mourn the closure of the frontier, suggesting that the nation must now grapple with finding new sources of energy, purpose, and growth.

subheader.text: Was the frontier really the defining feature of the country's identity?

subpoints.text: It depends who you ask. Turner believed frontier life forced settlers to be self-reliant and resourceful, fostering an American culture of individualism and democratic ideals. But Turner's thesis has been widely debated. Critics argue it oversimplifies the American experience and ignores the devastating impact on Native American communities. Native people experienced forced relocation, a loss of ancestral lands and sacred buffalo herds, and a profound disruption to indigenous ways of life.

, a widely respected naval officer and military historian. Read the passage describing some of Mahan's ideas. Then answer the question below.
Captain Alfred Mahan urged the U.S. to build a more powerful navy. His 1890 book,

content.text: The Influence of Sea Power upon History

pieces.text: , argued that a nation's economic prosperity, political influence, and military power depended on control of the world's seaways. He recruited and commanded the 1st United States Volunteer Cavalry, known as the "Rough Riders." Roosevelt and his regiment gained national fame for their role in the Battle of San Juan Hill in Cuba. The Rough Riders' charge up nearby Kettle Hill, while under heavy fire from Spanish troops, contributed to a decisive U.S. victory.

alternativeText.text: An illustration with three different scenes depicting Roosevelt with his signature round glasses and mustache with the Rough Riders in Cuba. The first panel shows Roosevelt standing outside a tent talking with other men with the caption "Colonel Roosevelt at his headquarters." The second image shows three men sitting on the ground cooking using basic tools with the caption "the cowboys coffee mill." The third image shows Roosevelt on horseback holding a gun and a sword. Roosevelt is at the front of a large group of soldiers as he leads them into battle.

label.text: The top left panel says, "Col. Roosevelt at his headquarters." The bottom left panel is a sketch of "the cowboys coffee mill." The circular panel shows Theodore Roosevelt in a cowboy hat and his signature round glasses on a horse in the Battle of San Juan Hill.

contents.text: The illustration depicts Roosevelt as a brave military leader who was able to handle harsh conditions. What details from the illustration support this characterization? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Roosevelt is shown living and cooking outdoors in a military camp.
Roosevelt is shown wearing round glasses.
Roosevelt is shown leading the Rough Riders into battle.
Roosevelt is shown riding a horse and holding weapons.

contents.text: Look back at the illustration. These choices are correct:

content.text: Roosevelt is shown living and cooking outdoors in a military camp.

explanationText.text: These details in the illustration show that Roosevelt, despite his wealthy background, was comfortable living in a tent and cooking at a "cowboy coffee mill." So, it demonstrates his ability to handle harsh conditions.

content.text: Roosevelt is shown leading the Rough Riders into battle.

explanationText.text: This detail in the illustration shows that Roosevelt didn't just order others into battle, but he was willing to face the same risks as the men he commanded. So, it demonstrates Roosevelt's bravery and leadership.

content.text: Roosevelt is shown riding a horse and holding weapons.

explanationText.text: This detail in the illustration shows that Roosevelt was an active participant in the battle. So, it demonstrates his bravery as a military leader.

contents.text: This choice is not correct:

content.text: Roosevelt is shown wearing round glasses.

explanationText.text: Roosevelt's round glasses were a part of his distinct personal style, but they are not relevant to his characterization as a brave military leader who was able to withstand harsh conditions.

contents.text: After the Spanish-American War, Theodore Roosevelt resumed his political career. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: Theodore Roosevelt returned from Cuba a national hero. A lifelong Republican, Roosevelt was recruited to run as his party's candidate for governor of New York. He won the election and quickly instituted a number of reforms designed to address unsafe working conditions and business and government corruption. These efforts were supported by members of the

, who wanted the government to help improve society through political and economic reforms. But Roosevelt's progressive politics put him at odds with conservative members of his party, who supported the interests of business and finance leaders over the interests of workers.

textContent.text: The anti-Roosevelt New York Republicans were relieved when President William McKinley chose Roosevelt as his running mate in 1900, since vice presidents typically had little power or influence over policies. However, Roosevelt only spent six months as vice president. In September 1901, Theodore Roosevelt became the 26th president of the United States after President McKinley was assassinated.

contents.text: In his first major speech as president, Theodore Roosevelt laid out his priorities in an address to Congress. Read an excerpt from the speech. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: When the Constitution was adopted, at the end of the eighteenth century, no human wisdom could foretell the sweeping changes, alike in industrial and political conditions, which were to take place by the beginning of the twentieth century…The conditions are now wholly different and wholly different action is called for…[The] old laws…are no longer sufficient.

We have now reached the point in the development of our interests where we are not only able to supply our own markets but to produce a constantly growing surplus for which we must find markets abroad…[The U.S. needs] to be able to secure the same respect for our rights from [other countries] which we are eager and anxious to extend to [them] in return, to insure fair treatment to us commercially, and to guarantee the safety of the American people.

in 1898, Theodore Roosevelt resigned from his position as assistant secretary of the Navy to join the war effort. He recruited and commanded the 1st United States Volunteer Cavalry, known as the "Rough Riders." Roosevelt and his regiment gained national fame for their role in the Battle of San Juan Hill in Cuba. contents.text: In his first major speech as president, Theodore Roosevelt laid out his priorities in an address to Congress. Read an excerpt from the speech. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: When the Constitution was adopted, at the end of the eighteenth century, no human wisdom could foretell the sweeping changes, alike in industrial and political conditions, which were to take place by the beginning of the twentieth century…The conditions are now wholly different and wholly different action is called for…[The] old laws…are no longer sufficient.

We have now reached the point in the development of our interests where we are not only able to supply our own markets but to produce a constantly growing surplus for which we must find markets abroad…[The U.S. needs] to be able to secure the same respect for our rights from [other countries] which we are eager and anxious to extend to [them] in return, to insure fair treatment to us commercially, and to guarantee the safety of the American people.

(1890–1920) was a period of reform in the United States that tried to address problems from the Gilded Age of the late 1800s. These problems included:

: The government avoided placing regulations on businesses, and many industries grew quickly. This growth created many factory jobs, but the lack of rules allowed companies to pay very low wages, create unsafe working conditions, and employ children. Industrialization also caused overcrowding, pollution, and the rise of powerful monopolies that limited competition.

: The Gilded Age featured extreme wealth inequality. A few powerful men gained immense wealth, while most urban workers and farmers struggled with poverty. African American people faced discrimination and violence, and women were denied basic rights like voting.

: The U.S. economy crashed multiple times during the Gilded Age, including the Panic of 1873 and the Panic of 1893, the two biggest economic crises before the Great Depression. These crashes caused high unemployment and widespread poverty.
: Political machines and powerful business leaders often controlled city and state governments through bribery, which weakened democracy and left the majority of citizens with little political power.

(1890–1920) was a period of reform in the United States that tried to address problems from the Gilded Age of the late 1800s. These problems included:

: The government avoided placing regulations on businesses, and many industries grew quickly. This growth created many factory jobs, but the lack of rules allowed companies to pay very low wages, create unsafe working conditions, and employ children. Industrialization also caused overcrowding, pollution, and the rise of powerful monopolies that limited competition.

: The Gilded Age featured extreme wealth inequality. A few powerful men gained immense wealth, while most urban workers and farmers struggled with poverty. African American people faced discrimination and violence, and women were denied basic rights like voting.

: The U.S. economy crashed multiple times during the Gilded Age, including the Panic of 1873 and the Panic of 1893, the two biggest economic crises before the Great Depression. These crashes caused high unemployment and widespread poverty.
: Political machines and powerful business leaders often controlled city and state governments through bribery, which weakened democracy and left the majority of citizens with little political power.

pieces.text: Progressive reformers faced economic and political opposition. Large business owners often opposed Progressive leaders because they did not want to be regulated or have their companies broken up into smaller businesses. Politicians often opposed Progressive attempts to reduce political corruption. This was especially true of members of

. Political machines were local political organizations such as Tammany Hall in New York City, which stayed in power by rewarding supporters for their loyalty. Some opponents accused Progressive reformers of supporting

, the Supreme Court ruled that a law limiting bakers to a 60-hour work week was unconstitutional. The Court also ruled against the first child labor regulations. Rulings like these often made reform very difficult to accomplish.

contents.text: Progressive Era reforms often grew out of new views about religion and government, but change was also spurred by major events. Read the passage about one such event. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: In 1909, workers at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory, a clothing manufacturer in New York, went on strike for higher pay and safer working conditions. The factory owners rejected workers' demands, claiming that they would be too costly.

Just over a year later, on March 25, 1911, a fire broke out at the factory. As flames engulfed the building, workers—mostly young women from immigrant communities—found that the exit doors were locked. Hundreds of people were trapped inside crowded rooms filled with fabric that quickly caught on fire. Bystanders watched, stunned, as workers jumped from windows and fell to their deaths. In total, 146 workers died from the fire.

The factory's owners were charged with manslaughter but were found not guilty after a brief trial. The lack of justice for the victims sparked public outrage and increased pressure on lawmakers to enact and enforce strict safety regulations on businesses.

content.text: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory was located on the top three floors of a ten-story building in New York City.

contents.text: Progressive Era reforms often grew out of new views about religion and government, but change was also spurred by major events. Read the passage about one such event. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: In 1909, workers at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory, a clothing manufacturer in New York, went on strike for higher pay and safer working conditions. The factory owners rejected workers' demands, claiming that they would be too costly.

Just over a year later, on March 25, 1911, a fire broke out at the factory. As flames engulfed the building, workers—mostly young women from immigrant communities—found that the exit doors were locked. Hundreds of people were trapped inside crowded rooms filled with fabric that quickly caught on fire. Bystanders watched, stunned, as workers jumped from windows and fell to their deaths. In total, 146 workers died from the fire.

The factory's owners were charged with manslaughter but were found not guilty after a brief trial. The lack of justice for the victims sparked public outrage and increased pressure on lawmakers to enact and enforce strict safety regulations on businesses.

content.text: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory was located on the top three floors of a ten-story building in New York City.

textContent.text: I am…unable to understand how Christianity, whether as a law or as a gospel, can be intelligently or adequately preached or lived in these days without a constant reference to social questions.…

contents.text: Progressive Era reforms were sometimes spurred by major events. Read the passage about one such event. Then answer the question below.

textContent.text: In 1909, workers at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory, a clothing manufacturer in New York, went on strike for higher pay and safer working conditions. The factory owners rejected workers' demands, claiming that they would be too costly.

Just over a year later, on March 25, 1911, a fire broke out at the factory. As flames engulfed the building, workers—mostly young women from immigrant communities—found that the exit doors were locked. Hundreds of people were trapped inside crowded rooms filled with fabric that quickly caught on fire. Bystanders watched, stunned, as workers jumped from windows and fell to their deaths. In total, 146 workers died from the fire.

The factory's owners were charged with manslaughter but were found not guilty after a brief trial. The lack of justice for the victims sparked public outrage and increased pressure on lawmakers to enact and enforce strict safety regulations on businesses.

content.text: The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory was located on the top three floors of a ten-story building in New York City.

, began to organize their reform movement. In 1851, Elizabeth Cady Stanton partnered with Susan B. Anthony, a skilled teacher and public speaker. contents.text: Black women faced unique struggles in the women's suffrage movement. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

content.text: Suffrage leader Nannie Burroughs, far left, attending the 1915 Banner State Woman's National Baptist Convention

textContent.text: White suffragists focused primarily on gender inequality, but Black women had to combat both race and gender discrimination. Black suffragist Frances Ellen Watkins Harper highlighted this reality when she told a white audience, "You white women speak here of rights. I speak of wrongs," referring to the additional dangers facing Black men and women. Similarly, Nannie Burroughs argued that Black women needed the right to vote not just for themselves but also to protect the entire Black community from racial violence.

Because they were often ignored or excluded by white-led groups, Black activists formed their own organizations. For example, Mary Church Terrell helped launch the National Association of Colored Women (NACW) in 1896, which addressed both racial and gender inequality. In 1913, when Illinois's state legislature granted women the right to vote in local elections, Ida B. Wells founded the Alpha Suffrage Club to encourage Black women in Chicago to vote.

textContent.text: White suffragists focused primarily on gender inequality, but Black women had to combat both race and gender discrimination. Black suffragist Frances Ellen Watkins Harper highlighted this reality when she told a white audience, "You white women speak here of rights. I speak of wrongs," referring to the additional dangers facing Black men and women. Similarly, Nannie Burroughs argued that Black women needed the right to vote not just for themselves but also to protect the entire Black community from racial violence.

Because they were often ignored or excluded by white-led groups, Black activists formed their own organizations. For example, Mary Church Terrell helped launch the National Association of Colored Women (NACW) in 1896, which addressed both racial and gender inequality. In 1913, when Illinois's state legislature granted women the right to vote in local elections, Ida B. Wells founded the Alpha Suffrage Club to encourage Black women in Chicago to vote.

in New York to address the legal, economic, and social inequalities women endured. There, Stanton and others drafted the Declaration of Sentiments, using language mirroring the Declaration of Independence to demand equality and suffrage.

staticItems.text: We hold these truths to be self-evident; that all men and women are created equal; that they are endowed by their Creator with certain inalienable rights….
The history of mankind is a history of repeated injuries and usurpations on the part of man toward woman, having in direct object the establishment of tyranny over her.
He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise. He has compelled her to submit to laws, in the formation of which she had no voice.
He has endeavored…to destroy her confidence in her own powers, to lessen her self-respect, and to make her willing to lead a dependent and abject life.

Now, in view of this entire disfranchisement of one-half the people of this country…we insist that they have immediate admission to all the rights and privileges which belong to them as citizens of these United States.

After the Seneca Falls Convention, women's voting right activists, often called

, began to organize their reform movement. In 1851, Elizabeth Cady Stanton partnered with Susan B. Anthony, a skilled teacher and public speaker. contents.text: Black women faced unique struggles in the women's suffrage movement. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

content.text: Suffrage leader Nannie Burroughs, far left, attending the 1915 Banner State Woman's National Baptist Convention

textContent.text: White suffragists focused primarily on gender inequality, but Black women had to combat both race and gender discrimination. Black suffragist Frances Ellen Watkins Harper highlighted this reality when she told a white audience, "You white women speak here of rights. I speak of wrongs," referring to the additional dangers facing Black men and women. Similarly, Nannie Burroughs argued that Black women needed the right to vote not just for themselves but also to protect the entire Black community from racial violence.

Because they were often ignored or excluded by white-led groups, Black activists formed their own organizations. For example, Mary Church Terrell helped launch the National Association of Colored Women (NACW) in 1896, which addressed both racial and gender inequality. In 1913, when Illinois's state legislature granted women the right to vote in local elections, Ida B. Wells founded the Alpha Suffrage Club to encourage Black women in Chicago to vote.

After the Seneca Falls Convention, women's voting right activists, often called

, began to organize their reform movement. In 1851, Elizabeth Cady Stanton partnered with Susan B. Anthony, a skilled teacher and public speaker. For the next 50 years, they led the movement together. Stanton defined the movement's goals, working behind the scenes to draft the documents and legal arguments that challenged the idea of women being inferior to men. Anthony traveled continuously across the country to deliver these ideas to the public, making her the most recognized figure of the struggle for women's rights.

When the Civil War ended and slavery was abolished, the women's suffrage movement faced new challenges. Read the passage. Then answer the question below.

pieces.text: In 1870, the women's suffrage movement reached a crossroads with the introduction of the

. This amendment guaranteed that the right to vote could not be denied "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude." While it was a landmark victory for Black men, it did not grant voting rights to women of any race.
Reformers like Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony refused to support the amendment. They argued that it was an injustice to grant the vote to all men while leaving all women

, meaning without the right to vote. But other women's suffrage reformers supported the amendment's passage. They feared that if they insisted on including women, the amendment would fail entirely and the opportunity to extend voting rights to Black men would be lost.
